::: {.lead-question}
Given one top-down RGB photo of a crop field, can a model place **one laser point on each weed**, so that
most weeds are hit and almost no crop plants are?
:::

## Question

**Why it matters.** A laser weeder destroys weeds without herbicide by heating the plant's growing point.
It needs a single aim point per weed — a bounding box is not enough, because the centre of a box around an
irregular weed can fall on bare soil or on the crop next to it. Every shot that lands on a crop damages
the harvest, so avoiding crops matters more than hitting every last weed.

**What is predicted, and when.** The prediction is made on the machine, frame by frame, as the camera passes
over the field. At that moment the only information is the **RGB image itself** — no species list, no stem
positions, no earlier frames.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Unit (one row)** | one plant instance (a weed or a crop) in one image; for the laser metrics, one shot |
| **Model output** | for every predicted weed: a pixel mask and one aim point (x, y) |
| **Target** | a shot is correct when its point lands inside a real weed and outside every crop |
| **Decision rule** | the laser fires only when the model is at least *X* sure a plant is a weed, and not within 20 px of a plant it thinks is a crop |
| **Main metrics** | share of weeds hit; share of shots that land on a crop; share of shots wasted on soil |

**Limits of the claim.** All evidence comes from offline photos: one main dataset recorded in European
fields with one camera, evaluated image by image. Nothing here is a field trial, says how much laser energy
kills a plant, or shows that the model works on other farms, crops or cameras. A small gallery of photos
from a different farm (Results) shows how quickly that can break.

## Data

**Main dataset: CropAndWeed** [@steininger2023cropandweed]. ${fmt(total("images"))} top-down RGB photos
(1920 × 1088 px, about 0.4 mm per pixel) of crop rows with weeds, recorded in
${fmt(total("sessions"))} recording sessions. It is one of the few public datasets that label **both crops and
weeds**, which this question needs: a weeds-only dataset cannot tell us whether the laser would hit a crop.

- **Annotations:** a box and stem position for every plant, plus a pixel mask that gives each pixel its
  species. We use the authors' own two-class variant *CropOrWeed2*: **Crop** (maize, sugar beet, soybean,
  sunflower, potato, pea, bean, pumpkin) and **Weed** (57 weed species).
- **Two recording sets:** *ave* = the Application set (real farm fields) and *vwg* = the Experimental set
  (test plots). Real fields are the harder, more realistic case.
- **Access limits:** non-commercial use only, and **no redistribution** of images or annotations. The data
  is downloaded from the official source in each run, and **no CropAndWeed photo appears on this site** —
  only statistics and model outputs.

**Quality issues that shape the method.**

1. **Plants outside the two classes.** ${fmt(total("ignored"))} annotated plants
   (${pct(total("ignored") / (total("ignored") + total("crop") + total("weed")))} of all) are species
   outside CropOrWeed2 or are labelled only "Vegetation" because the annotators could not identify them.
   They are kept as **ignore regions**: a prediction on them counts neither as right nor wrong.
2. **Masks are per class, not per plant.** Two touching weeds share one blob of "weed" pixels, but the laser
   needs one point per plant. *Preprocessing* explains how the plants are separated.
3. **Many plants are tiny.** Weeds outnumber crops about ${(total("weed") / total("crop")).toFixed(1)} to 1, and
   ${pct((dataset.sizes.Weed["0–16"] + dataset.sizes.Weed["16–24"]) / Object.values(dataset.sizes.Weed).reduce((a, b) => a + b))}
   of weeds are at most 24 px across (about 1 cm) — a few pixels once the image is shrunk for the network.
4. **Near-duplicate frames.** Consecutive photos in a session overlap heavily, so a random split would put
   almost the same image in training and test.
5. **Imbalanced crops.** A few crop species dominate (chart below); rare ones are harder to learn.

**Earlier dataset: CottonWeedDet12** [@lu2023cottonweeddet12; @dang2023yoloweeds]. 5,648 photos from US
cotton fields with boxes for 12 weed species. The first experiments used it, but it labels **no crops**, so
it can show weed finding but not crop safety. That gap is why the project moved to CropAndWeed; five of its
photos still appear in the gallery.

## Preprocessing

All steps are deterministic rules or come from the dataset itself; **no statistic is fitted on the data**, so
nothing can leak from validation or test into training.

1. **Labels → two classes.** Each species id is mapped to Crop or Weed with the official CropOrWeed2 table;
   unmapped species and "Vegetation" become ignore regions.
2. **Per-plant masks.** For each plant box, the mask is the class's pixels inside that box. Where that is
   ambiguous — two overlapping boxes of the same class, or a box with no class pixels — the image is passed to
   SAM 2.1 [@ravi2024sam2] with the box as a prompt, and SAM's mask is cut back to the class's pixels, so
   SAM can only split plants, never invent leaves. Each mask is stored as its largest outline (polygon).
3. **Split by recording session, before any model is trained.** Whole sessions go to train / validation /
   test (65 / 20 / 15 % of images, seed 42), so near-duplicate frames never cross splits. The split is
   fixed in `configs/datasets/cropandweed.yaml` and rebuilt identically on every machine.
4. **Model input.** Images are resized to the model's input size (1024 or 1280 px wide, aspect kept) and
   scaled to 0–1 by dividing by 255 — a fixed rule, not a learned normalisation.
5. **Augmentation (training only).** Random mosaics, scale and colour jitter and horizontal flips;
   experiment 5 adds vertical flips and ±15° rotations, since a top-down photo is equally valid upside down.

**Who sees which split.** Training uses *train* only. *Validation* picks the best training epoch, the model
and the laser's confidence threshold. *Test* is used once, at the very end (Evaluation).

## Baseline and methods

### Baseline: "every green blob is a weed"

Without machine learning, a weeder could aim at anything green. The baseline computes the vegetation index
ExG − ExR [@meyer2008exgr] on brightness-normalised colours and keeps pixels where it is positive (its
published threshold, no tuning), cleans specks with a 3 × 3 opening, and treats **every connected blob of at
least 64 px** (8 × 8, smaller than the smallest labelled plants) as a weed, aimed at with the same point
method as the model. It cannot tell crops from weeds, so it has no crop safety gate. If a trained model is
worth having, it must beat this on crop safety without losing too many weeds.

The textbook ExG index with an Otsu threshold [@woebbecke1995exg] was tried first, on two validation images
only: the greenish tint of the soil in these photos turned it into hundreds of soil fragments per image, so
the published ExG − ExR rule replaced it.

### Model: YOLO11s-seg instance segmentation

YOLO11s-seg [@jocher2024yolo11] is a one-stage instance-segmentation network (10 M parameters). For every
detected plant it predicts a box, a class score (Crop / Weed) and 32 mask coefficients that are combined with
shared prototype masks into a pixel mask. It starts from weights pretrained on everyday photos (COCO) and is
fine-tuned on CropAndWeed.

- **Objective:** a sum of box-regression loss, class loss (binary cross-entropy) and per-pixel mask loss,
  minimised with AdamW for up to 80 epochs; training stops early when validation accuracy has not improved
  for 20 epochs, and the best validation epoch is kept.
- **Why this method:** the laser needs one point *per plant*, so plain semantic segmentation (one class per
  pixel) is not enough, and a box alone puts the aim point off the plant. A one-stage model runs in real time
  on a modest GPU, unlike two-stage models such as Mask R-CNN [@he2017maskrcnn].
- **Assumptions:** a top-down view at a fixed height, plants visible (not hidden under leaves), labels that are
  right on average, and test fields that look like training fields. The gallery tests the last one.
- **Three trained candidates:** exp 3 at 1024 px input, exp 4 at 1280 px (small weeds get more pixels),
  exp 5 at 1280 px with vertical flips and rotations. A fourth run at full 1920 px did not finish in time.

### From mask to laser point

The aim point is the mask pixel that maximises *(distance to the mask's edge) × (a Gaussian around the mask's
centre, width = half the plant's radius)*: it always lies inside the plant, near its centre, and not on a
thin leaf tip. Simpler rules fail in predictable ways — the centre of mass can fall between the leaves of a
star-shaped weed, and the box centre can fall on soil.

### Crop safety gate

A shot is vetoed when its point lies within **20 px (about 8 mm)** of a plant the model predicts as a crop —
roughly the laser spot radius plus aiming error. The gate can only protect crops the model actually
recognises; the Errors section shows what that means in practice.
